idiom_name: no reader-writer lock in a single-threaded realm; Web Locks (mode 'shared'/'exclusive') or a promise-chain mutex serialises writers
implementation_notes: A JavaScript realm runs one thread, so concurrent readers of the same object cannot exist and no read lock can be contended; a reader-writer lock would import blocking semantics the runtime does not have (Atomics.wait throws on the main thread). Cross-realm coordination is asynchronous instead: the Web Locks API takes mode: 'shared' for concurrent readers and the default 'exclusive' for a writer, releasing automatically when the callback settles; inside one process a promise-chain mutex or an async queue serialises writers while readers simply read the single owner's state. The classic structure is justified only when several worker_threads share a SharedArrayBuffer and readers must block while a writer runs - and only inside workers, never on the main thread.
pitfalls: Atomics.wait cannot be used on the main thread (it throws), so a blocking reader-writer lock cannot exist where UI work happens.
Web Locks is asynchronous and origin-scoped: a lock held across an await blocks other tabs, and it gives no protection inside synchronous code.
A promise-chain mutex only serialises the tasks that go through it; synchronous code between awaits still interleaves, and one rejected promise can wedge the chain.
worker_threads share memory only through SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics; ordinary objects are structured-cloned, so a 'shared' reader-writer lock over them is an illusion.
alternative: Keep the mutable state in one owner (the event loop or a single worker) where readers need no lock at all, exchange copies by message passing (structured clone) or immutable snapshots, and serialise writers asynchronously with a promise-chain mutex or the Web Locks API (mode 'shared' for readers, 'exclusive' for the writer); use SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics only inside workers when memory sharing is unavoidable.
